case_study_insert.main_stem: Almond Grove Nut Company (AGN) is a cooperative in the tree-nut farming and processing sector, based in a dry inland valley and employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 1998 by a group of growers led by Tomas Bergström, it supplies shelled almonds to health-food wholesalers and operates a flat structure with democratic leadership. AGN plans to invest $690,000 in a new shelling and packing facility, financed by a $390,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $225,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.80 a unit and a selling price of $9.30, and currently produces 100,000 units a year. AGN faces rising quality rejects: 3.6% of packs fail inspection and labour turnover is increasing.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The shelling line processed 26,400 units last quarter with a reject rate of 3.6%, down from 5.1% a year ago. Customer returns fell from 33 to 19 per month. Average dispatch time is 3.8 days. A survey of 420 buyers found that 72% would pay up to $0.45 more for residue-free almonds, and 58% check country-of-origin labels. Records show 14 of 50 members have not completed on-the-job training on the new optical sorters; off-the-job training courses at the agricultural college cost $950 per member.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Almond Grove Nut Company as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 4.75%, increasing borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $12.30 to $13.05 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale nut and packaging input costs have risen 8.7% year-on-year, food inflation is 5.2%, and consumer spending on health-food snacks grew 3.3%.

questions.question_text: AGN plans to fund part of its shelling-facility expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for AGN of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs AGN no interest or capital repayments, protecting the cash flow of a cooperative that already carries fixed costs of $225,000 a year and a variable cost of $4.80 a unit. The $300,000 of retained profit is generated by the grower members themselves, so money that would have gone to the $390,000 bank loan can instead be used to cut the 3.6% reject rate on the new optical sorters or to absorb the 8.7% rise in nut and packaging costs.

Point 2: Using retained profit keeps control with the grower members led by Tomas Bergström, since no lender can impose conditions on how the $690,000 shelling and packing facility is run. This matters for a cooperative with democratic leadership where members expect a say in decisions. It also avoids the collateral and default risk of the bank loan: if health-food wholesalers cut orders, the facility cannot be repossessed, and the project can start at once without waiting for loan approval while the 26,400-unit quarterly throughput is maintained.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to AGN and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: AGN is launching a new residue-free almond range. Consider trade fair exhibitions, local radio advertising, or social media influencer marketing. Which should AGN choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Trade fair exhibitions: Food fairs let AGN demonstrate residue-free almonds to health-food wholesalers face to face, answer questions about country of origin and win listings directly — valuable when 58% of 420 surveyed buyers check origin labels. However, stand fees, travel and staff time are costly for a cooperative funding a $690,000 facility, and each fair reaches only a limited number of buyers.

Local radio advertising: Radio is relatively cheap and can repeatedly reach listeners in the dry inland valley and nearby towns, building awareness of the new range. Its weakness is that AGN sells to health-food wholesalers well beyond one local area, and radio cannot show the residue-free certification or the product itself, so it is a poor fit for a 72% premium segment that wants proof.

Social media influencer marketing: Health-food and cooking influencers can show the almonds and explain residue-free certification visually, reaching the exact buyers identified in the survey at modest cost with measurable engagement. Credibility must be protected and results take time to build, but the message can be shared nationally and adapted quickly.

Recommendation: AGN should choose social media influencer marketing, backed by selected trade fairs for wholesale buyers. It reaches the researched 72% premium segment and demonstrates origin credentials that radio cannot show. Radio is rejected as too narrow and unable to prove certification; trade fairs alone are rejected as too expensive and limited in reach for a 50-member cooperative with a $390,000 loan to service.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of AGN with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of AGN with a well-justified recommendation explaining why radio and trade fairs are rejected.

questions.question_text: AGN's reject rate is 3.6% and labour turnover is rising. Explain two benefits for AGN of using democratic leadership to improve motivation among its grower-members.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the 50 grower-members share decisions about how the new shelling and packing facility is organised, which suits a cooperative and raises commitment. Members who help set inspection routines are more likely to take the 3.6% reject problem seriously, offering practical ideas that can build on the fall from 5.1% to 3.6% and protect the $9.30 selling price to health-food wholesalers.

Point 2: Involvement gives members a voice in shift planning and training, which can reduce the rising labour turnover and the disruption it causes on a 100,000-unit line with fixed costs of $225,000 a year. Because 14 of 50 members still need on-the-job training on the optical sorters, consulting those who operate the equipment helps target that training properly while the $690,000 facility beds in and the $390,000 loan is serviced.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to AGN's quality, staffing and output.

questions.question_text: AGN must upskill 14 members to operate the new optical sorters. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the agricultural college. Which should AGN choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching the 14 members beside the optical sorters is directly relevant to AGN's own inspection standards and costs no course fees, unlike the $950 per member charged by the agricultural college. It keeps all 14 members productive while they learn, protecting the 26,400 units processed last quarter and the fall in rejects from 5.1% to 3.6%. The drawback is that member-trainers have their own shelling work to do, and bad habits may spread without formal testing.

Off-the-job training: The $950 per member college course gives structured teaching and a recognised certificate for all 14 members, costing $13,300 in total — affordable against a $690,000 investment. It takes 14 of 50 members away from the line, reducing short-term capacity, and the generic content may not match AGN's sorter settings, so follow-up coaching would still be needed to cut rejects further.

Decision: AGN should choose on-the-job training first, with short college modules later for the most senior operators. It is cheaper, machine-specific and protects output while the reject rate is only just improving; full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing $13,300 and 14 of 50 members from the line would disrupt supply to health-food wholesalers when a $390,000 loan must be serviced.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to AGN.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of AGN.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of AGN with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how AGN's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $225,000 ÷ ($9.30 − $4.80) = $225,000 ÷ $4.50 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $9.30 − $4.80 = $4.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways AGN's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 50,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 100,000 units, giving a margin of safety of 50,000 units, to judge whether the $690,000 shelling facility is fully utilised.
2. Contribution per unit of $4.50 lets AGN model the $0.45 premium: if 72% of surveyed buyers accept it, managers can estimate the extra contribution and weigh it against the 8.7% input-cost rise.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $225,000 and contribution helps set the volume needed to service interest on the $390,000 bank loan before the cooperative borrows more.
4. Unit cost can be checked as $225,000 ÷ 100,000 + $4.80 = $7.05, and labour productivity as 100,000 units ÷ 50 members = 2,000 units per member, giving benchmarks to monitor the 3.6% reject rate and rising labour turnover.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 50,000 units vs 100,000 output; the $0.45 premium against $225,000 fixed costs; loan servicing on the $390,000 bank loan; and unit cost of $7.05 with labour productivity of 2,000 units per member.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate AGN's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has AGN's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.40 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.50 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.91 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.11 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $88,000 inventories + $112,000 trade receivables + $52,000 cash = $252,000; 2025 current assets = $70,000 + $125,000 + $75,000 = $270,000. Dividing by current liabilities of $180,000 in both years gives 2024 = $252,000 ÷ $180,000 = 1.40 and 2025 = $270,000 ÷ $180,000 = 1.50. Excluding inventories gives 2024 = ($252,000 − $88,000) ÷ $180,000 = $164,000 ÷ $180,000 = 0.91 and 2025 = ($270,000 − $70,000) ÷ $180,000 = $200,000 ÷ $180,000 = 1.11.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. The 2024 figure of 1.40 rose to 1.50 because current assets grew from $252,000 to $270,000 while current liabilities stayed at $180,000; cash rose from $52,000 to $75,000. The inventory-excluding measure rose from 0.91 to 1.11, so AGN can now cover short-term obligations without relying on selling almond stock — important while it services a $390,000 loan and funds a $690,000 facility. Receivables did rise from $112,000 to $125,000, tying up cash, so credit control with health-food wholesalers matters; inventories fell to $70,000, which supports the 26,400-unit quarterly throughput but leaves little buffer if the 3.6% reject rate worsens.

Conclusion: AGN's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the gain does not depend on inventory. The residual risk is slower-paying wholesalers, so members should tighten collection while the new facility operates.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether AGN's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for AGN of introducing residue-free certification for its almonds.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Residue-free certification matches the 72% of 420 surveyed buyers who would pay up to $0.45 more, helping AGN defend its $4.50 contribution per unit while nut and packaging inputs rise 8.7%. It also appeals to the 58% who check country-of-origin labels, strengthening the cooperative's relationship with health-food wholesalers and supporting the $690,000 shelling facility.

Disadvantage: Certification and the testing it requires add costs that could push up the $4.80 variable cost per unit unless the $0.45 premium is accepted across the full range. A failed inspection batch would add to the current 3.6% reject rate and cut the 26,400 units processed each quarter, while fixed costs of $225,000 continue regardless of output.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to AGN's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 6.1% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in nut and packaging input costs will affect AGN. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 4.75%): The base rate rises by 0.75 percentage points. If the $390,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the additional annual interest is 0.0075 × $390,000 = $2,925 a year, which is modest against fixed costs of $225,000 a year; if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Higher rates could make health-food wholesalers cautious about premium stock orders, but AGN can largely remove the direct effect by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (6.1%, from $12.30 to $13.05 per hour): This pushes up the wage bill for a 50-member cooperative and cannot be avoided. No hours worked or individual pay rates are given in the insert, so an annual total would be an invention. The comparison that can be derived is productivity: 100,000 units ÷ 50 members = 2,000 units per member. If that is sustained the rise is manageable; if labour turnover continues to rise and throughput falls, unit labour cost increases and the $4.50 contribution per unit is reduced.

Input cost inflation (8.7% on nuts and packaging): The insert does not decompose the $4.80 variable cost, so only a labelled bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 8.7%, the addition is 0.087 × $4.80 = $0.42 per unit, and at 100,000 units a year that is about $41,760. This is an upper bound, not a prediction; the true effect depends on the nut share of variable cost, which is not stated. AGN can recover part via the $0.45 residue-free premium accepted by 72% of surveyed buyers.

Conclusion: The 8.7% input-cost rise will have the greatest impact because it applies to every unit and directly erodes the $4.50 contribution that supports the $690,000 facility. The interest effect of $2,925 is small and fixable, and the wage effect can be softened if 2,000-units-per-member productivity holds, so input-cost inflation requires the strongest management response.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to AGN.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on AGN's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of AGN with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
